Learning Objectives
Define and assess pelvic stability.
Explain the usefulness of the Tile classification system and the Young-Burgess classification
system in predicting stability of the pelvic ring.
Discuss the role of an examination under anesthesia with regard to determining pelvic ring
stability.
Describe the treatment options available for stabilization of various anterior and posterior
pelvic ring injury patterns.
Identify and describe the features of a normal and dysmorphic sacrum and their effects on
fixation options for the posterior pelvic ring.
Summarize current outcomes in the management of pelvic ring injuries.

Introduction
Surgical Versus Nonsurgical Management
The primary determinant of the need for surgical management is instability.

Surgical Versus Nonsurgical Management
Stability can be broadly defined as the ability of the pelvic ring’s to resist deformity, heal,
and have resolution of pain during physiologic loading postinjury. Unfortunately, no
universally agreed on criteria are available for deciding whether an injury is stable or
unstable. Currently, surgeons use the mechanism of injury, injury pattern, and dynamic
stress imaging (examination under anesthesia) to predict or gauge stability and the need
for fixation.
Injury Pattern
The Tile classification system and the Young-Burgess classification system can be used as a
framework to predict stability and the need for surgical treatment.
The Tile classification system is shown in (Table 1;.Resource 1)

Tile type A—The pelvic ring and the sciatic buttress are intact; therefore, these injuries are
inherently stable. Apart from widely displaced iliac wing fractures, they usually can be
managed nonsurgically.
Tile type B—These injuries are associated with varying degrees of rotational (internal or
external) instability but not vertical instability. Depending on the degree of rotational
instability, injuries in this category may be managed surgically or nonsurgically.

Tile type C—These injuries are rotationally and vertically unstable. Most require surgical
reduction and fixation to achieve sufficient stability to allow for mobilization and prevent
malunion and/or nonunion.
The Young-Burgess classification system is shown in (Figure 1)
Figure 1 Illustrations show the Young-Burgess classification of pelvic fractures. A, Anterior-
posterior compression (APC) type I. B, APC type II. C, APC type III. D, Lateral compression (LC)
type I. E, LC type II. F, LC type III. G, Vertical shear. The arrow in each panel indicates the
direction of force producing the fracture pattern. (Copyright Jesse B. Jupiter, MD, Boston, MA,
and Bruce D. Browner, MD, Mebane, NC.)

Injury Pattern
Anterior-posterior compression (APC) injuries are subclassified as APC type I, type II, and
type III, indicating increasing severity of injury and instability. They are characterized by
external rotation resulting from an anterior-to-posterior directed force vector. All injuries
begin as APC type I and progress through to APC type II and APC type III as increasing
amounts of force continue to be applied.
APC type I injuries (Figure 2), as originally described, consist of a symphyseal injury with
minor diastasis and minimal to no posterior sacroiliac injury. The sacrotuberous,
sacrospinous, and sacroiliac ligaments, as well as the pelvic floor are intact. If the
surgeon is confident that the injury is a true APC type I injury, nonsurgical management
is the standard accepted treatment option.

Figure 2 AP radiograph obtained on presentation (A) and axial CT scan obtained after
the application of a pelvic binder (B) of the pelvis of a patient with an anterior-posterior
compression type I injury. Obvious mild widening of the pubic symphysis and the right
sacroiliac joint are observed but were largely reduced with binder placement. (Courtesy
of Paul Toogood, MD, San Francisco, CA, and Reza Firoozabadi, MD, Seattle, WA.)
APC type II injuries consist of moderate symphyseal diastasis and a partial sacroiliac joint
injury. The sacrotuberous, sacrospinous, and anterior sacroiliac ligaments are disrupted
along with the pelvic floor, with varying degrees of injury to the posterior sacroiliac
ligament complex. Management includes reduction and stabilization of the anterior
pelvic ring (symphysis, usually), with or without reduction and stabilization of the
posterior pelvic ring (sacroiliac joint, usually).
APC type III injuries (Figure 3) consist of complete disruption of the symphysis,
sacrotuberous, sacrospinous, and sacroiliac ligaments, as well as the pelvic floor. This
injury typically is characterized by widening of the symphysis and the anterior and
posterior aspect of the sacroiliac joint. Although potential for cranial (vertical)
displacement exists, this injury is characterized by wide lateral displacement of the
injured hemipelvis. Management typically involves open reduction and internal fixation
of the anterior and posterior pelvic ring injuries.

Figure 3 Axial CT scan of a pelvis with an anterior-posterior compression type III injury to
the left sacroiliac joint. Note the translation of the entire ilium away from the sacrum,
indicating no sacroiliac ligaments remain intact. (Courtesy of Paul Toogood, MD, San
Francisco, CA, and Reza Firoozabadi, MD, Seattle, WA.)
Lateral compression injuries are subclassified into lateral compression type I, type II, and
type III. They are characterized by an internal rotation deformity resulting from a lateral-
to-medial force vector. Dissimilar from APC injuries, the increasing numeric grade does
not represent a progression of severity, and various injury patterns and severities exist
within each subcategory. Dissimilar from APC injuries, simply describing an injury as
lateral compression type I or lateral compression type II rarely provides adequate
information to direct management.
Lateral compression type I injuries typically consist of internal rotation of the injured
hemipelvis associated with rami fractures in the anterior pelvic ring and a sacral alar
fracture in the posterior pelvic ring. Unless substantial internal rotational deformity is
present, the only radiographic findings are anterior rami fractures identified on an AP
pelvis view. All patients with an anterior pelvic ring injury on an AP pelvis radiograph
should undergo CT to rule out an associated posterior pelvic ring injury. Pelvic fractures
classified as lateral compression type I encompass a broad spectrum of injury and
instability, with some fractures requiring open reduction internal fixation and other
fractures being managed nonsurgically. To some degree, they can be separated based
on the extent of the sacral fracture; however, many other factors contribute to the
overall level of instability.

Lateral compression type I injuries with an incomplete sacral fracture (Figure 4) are
common injuries sustained in geriatric and younger patient populations. In addition to
the anterior pelvic rami fractures, CT scans will show an impaction fracture involving the
anterior cortex of the sacrum that does not completely traverse the sacrum to exit the
posterior cortex. These injuries usually are stable and can be managed via pain control,
mobilization with physical therapy, and weight bearing as tolerated. Surgeons must
recognize the rare instance in which the anterior sacral fracture exits into the sacroiliac
joint rather than the posterior cortex of the sacrum because this represents a higher
degree of instability consistent with a complete sacral fracture.
Figure 4 Axial CT scan of a pelvis with a lateral compression type I pelvic ring injury, with
an incomplete sacral fracture and buckling of the anterior sacral ala (arrow). (Courtesy of
Paul Toogood, MD, San Francisco, CA, and Reza Firoozabadi, MD, Seattle, WA.)
Lateral compression type I injuries with a complete sacral fracture and minimal
displacement (Figure 5) may present as various combinations of anterior pelvic rami
fractures associated with a sacral fracture line that traverses the entire sacrum from the
anterior cortex to the posterior cortex. Management of these injuries is controversial
and depends, in part, on the degree of internal rotation deformity observed on
presentation and the constellation of injuries to the anterior pelvic ring (unilateral or
bilateral injury). Nonsurgical management via protected–weight bearing and close

MD, Seattle, WA.)
In lateral compression type I injuries with a complete sacral fracture and displacement
(Figure 6), the anterior pelvic rami fractures are associated with a complete sacral
fracture that is displaced and demonstrates multiplanar deformity (flexion and
translation in addition to the internal rotation). Management of these injuries typically
requires surgical reduction and fixation via open and percutaneous techniques.

complete, displaced fracture of the left sacral ala. (Courtesy of Paul Toogood, MD, San
Francisco, CA, and Reza Firoozabadi, MD, Seattle, WA.)
Lateral compression type II injuries typically consist of internal rotation of the injured
hemipelvis associated with rami fractures in the anterior pelvic ring and an iliac wing
fracture of the posterior pelvic ring. These injuries can be further subdivided based on
the location of the iliac wing fracture.
In lateral compression type II iliac fractures with an intact sacroiliac joint (Figure 7), the
fulcrum, or axis of rotation, is anterior to the sacroiliac joint, creating a fracture through
the ilium that starts at the iliac crest and exits the sciatic buttress just anterior to the
sacroiliac joint. These injuries are associated with varying degrees of displacement and
comminution that can be managed nonsurgically or require open reduction and internal
fixation (Resource 2).

Figure 7 Axial CT scan of a pelvis with a lateral compression type II fracture, with fracture
through the left ilium. This is a classic crescent fracture (arrow), which occurred anterior
to the sacroiliac joint. Fixation may include open plating and/or the use of a lateral
compression type II screw along the corridor between the anterior inferior iliac spine
and the posterior superior iliac spine. (Courtesy of Paul Toogood, MD, San Francisco, CA,
and Reza Firoozabadi, MD, Seattle, WA.)
In lateral compression type II iliac fractures with disruption of the sacroiliac joint (Figure
8), the axis of rotation is within the sacroiliac joint, creating a fracture of the iliac wing
that enters the sacroiliac joint. Typically, the anterior sacroiliac joint is disrupted, and a
small portion of the iliac wing is left attached to the sacrum via the posterior sacroiliac
ligament complex (the so-called crescent fragment). These injuries usually are unstable
and require surgical reduction and stabilization. Fixation strategies depend on the
location of the iliac fracture line and the size of the crescent fragment. Large crescent
fragments with minimal sacroiliac joint involvement are managed similar to iliac wing
fractures, whereas those with small iliac fragments and considerable sacroiliac joint
involvement are managed similar to sacroiliac joint dislocations.

Lateral compression type III injuries (Figure 9) consist of an internal rotation injury
(lateral compression type I or lateral compression type II) of the ipsilateral hemipelvis
associated with an external rotation injury (APC) of the contralateral pelvis. Occasionally,
these injuries are referred to as a wind-swept pelvis. These injuries are inherently
unstable and require surgical management via reduction and fixation of both sides of
the pelvis.

Vertical shear injuries result from a fall from height and consist of any combination of
anterior (rami fractures or symphyseal dislocation) and posterior (sacral fracture, iliac
fracture, or sacroiliac joint dislocation) pelvic ring injury. Multiplanar deformity is
associated with the defining feature of the injured hemipelvis being displaced cranially
(Figure 10).

Combined mechanism injuries are a final grouping of pelvic fracture in which
radiographic deformity does not clearly represent one dominant force vector, and
multiple fracture patterns and deforming forces coexist. Both vertical shear and
combined mechanism pelvic ring injuries are highly unstable, are associated with
substantial blood loss and morbidity, and require surgical reduction and stabilization for
resuscitation and definitive management.

Examination Under Anesthesia

Examination Under Anesthesia
Although radiographs and CT scans provide some insight into pelvic stability, they are
static images and do not always depict the true degree of potential instability. Elastic
recoil of the hemipelvis, pelvic binders, and the concave nature of the table in the CT
scanner may further confound the interpretation of these static images. By definition,
stability is ultimately determined by loading the pelvic ring and evaluating for
displacement over time. Therefore, the use of dynamic stress imaging has been
suggested as an adjunct to aid in a more accurate determination of instability in patients
in whom it may not be readily apparent.3 These examinations are performed in the
operating room with the patient under sedation or anesthetic, obtaining AP, inlet, and

Definitive Management

Definitive Management
After an unstable pelvic ring injury has been diagnosed, the surgeon needs to carefully
evaluate all elements of the injury pattern and the osseous anatomy of the pelvic ring.
The injury can be divided into an anterior ring component and a posterior ring
component; anterior ring injuries include any combination of rami fractures and
dislocation of the pubic symphysis, and posterior ring injuries include any combination
of injury to the sacrum, the sacroiliac joint, and the ilium. Bilateral pelvic ring injuries are
not uncommon, with one being subtle and easily overlooked, particularly if the primary
injury is substantial.

Effective definitive treatment of patients with a pelvic ring injury requires effective and
efficient communication between multiple medical and surgical disciplines:
trauma/critical care surgeons, urologic surgeons, orthopaedic surgeons, interventional
radiologists, urologists, and intensivists. Knowledge of previous surgery to the abdomen,
pelvis, or urogenital tract (historically or during the course of resuscitation and acute
management) and the extent of angiographic intervention is critical in determining
optimal surgical approaches and reduction techniques.
The foundations of surgical reduction and fixation are based on the following tenets:
Restore normal anatomy to preserve function.
Provide adequate stability to allow for healing without loss of reduction.
Respect the soft tissues and associated soft-tissue injuries.
More points of fixation generally lead to increased stability.
Not all points of injury need fixation all the time.
Open reduction of the anterior pelvic ring may aid in reduction of the posterior pelvic
ring.
General Philosophy
Historically, Tile type B injuries (lateral compression type I, lateral compression type II, APC
type II) that result in partial instability of the pelvis (uniaxial rotationally unstable) can be
successfully managed via anterior-only fixation (Resource 3).
For lateral compression injuries, application of fixation that resists internal rotation (an
anterior distraction external fixator, retrograde ramus screws, or plating of the ramus fracture)
is adequate in most patients.
For APC injuries, application of fixation that resists external rotation (symphyseal plating)
generally is adequate.

As the degree of instability increases and multiplanar deformity presents in Tile type C
injuries (complete displaced lateral compression type I or lateral compression type II,
lateral compression type III, APC type III, vertical shear, and combined mechanism), then
combinations of anterior and posterior fixation are required to maintain reduction and
prevent malunion or nonunion. In such patients, initial open or closed reduction of the
anterior pelvic ring may help to improve alignment of the posterior pelvic ring to the
extent that percutaneous indirect reduction and fixation is all that is required for the
posterior pelvic ring. This is particularly advantageous in patients with major soft-tissue
trauma that would ordinarily preclude open techniques to approach the posterior pelvis.
More controversially, unstable lateral compression (internal rotation) injuries without
flexion or extension deformity of the posterior pelvic ring are increasingly being
managed via posterior-only percutaneous fixation followed by an examination under
anesthesia to determine the need for supplemental anterior fixation in the form of
percutaneous fixation rami screws, plating, or placement of an external fixator.4
Various approaches and fixation options are available for surgical reduction and
stabilization of pelvic ring injuries. Ideally, closed or percutaneous reduction techniques
should be attempted before proceeding to open reduction; however, reduction quality
within 1 cm of anatomic reduction correlates with overall improved functional results
and outcomes.5 Therefore, if closed reduction attempts fail to adequately correct the
deformity and soft-tissue conditions permit, open reduction should be performed.
A Pfannenstiel incision with a vertical midline split of the rectus abdominus is the most
common approach used to gain access to the anterior pelvic ring (pubic symphysis and
the superior rami). A horizontal and slightly curved incision is made 1 to 2 cm cranial to
the pubic symphysis, subcutaneous tissue is elevated off the anterior rectus fascia, and
the linea alba is identified and incised. The bladder is protected via Foley catheter
drainage, packing the retropubic space, and gentle retraction. Exposure of the anterior
pelvis can be performed beginning at the pubic symphysis and working laterally by
releasing the iliopectineal fascia and pectineus muscle from the posterosuperior aspect
of the ramus as far as the pubic eminence. This dissection can be carried further
posteriorly along the pelvic brim to the supracetabular bone or sacroiliac joint as
necessary. The corona mortis is encountered approximately 5 to 6 cm lateral to the

pubic symphysis; however, this may be variable, especially in patients with severe
displacement of the hemipelvis.
If the patient is in the supine position, the posterior pelvic ring can be approached from
anterior using the lateral or iliac window (window No. 1) of the ilioinguinal approach. This
approach can be used to obtain access to iliac wing fractures and sacroiliac joint
dislocations but not sacral fractures because of an increased risk of injury to the L5
nerve root. The incision starts at the anterior superior iliac spine and is extended
posteriorly for approximately 15 cm along the crest. The interval between the tensor
fascia and the external oblique is developed, and the external oblique fascia is released
from the crest. Next, subperiosteal elevation of the iliacus is performed to expose the
internal iliac fossa. The knee and hip should be flexed to decrease tension on the
iliopsoas muscle and aid in visualization of the sacroiliac joint.
Posterior approaches to the pelvic ring vary depending on the specific injury that is being
addressed and the type of fixation that will be used. Sacral fractures can be exposed via
a typical midline (bilateral sacral fractures) or paramedian (unilateral sacral fracture)
incision from L5 to the distal sacrum with elevation of the paraspinal musculature from
medial to lateral. Sacroiliac joint dislocations and iliac fractures are exposed via a
curvilinear incision along the posterior iliac crest to the posterior inferior iliac spine, with
elevation of the gluteal musculature from medial to lateral.
Anterior Pelvic Ring Reduction and Fixation Techniques

Anterior Pelvic Ring Reduction and Fixation Techniques
Displaced rami fractures typically are reduced with the use of pointed reduction clamps
and stabilized with the use of a medullary implant, such as an antegrade/retrograde
ramus screw, or a pelvic reconstruction plate, depending on the fracture pattern and
location and whether the medullary anatomy of the ramus can safely accommodate a
medullary screw (Figures 13,14 ; Video 1).
The surgeon should be mindful of the location of the contralateral spermatic cord in
male patients, which has been shown to be within 18 mm of instrumentation.6 The

The pubic symphysis can be reduced with the use of a large Weber clamp placed
anteriorly on the pubic tubercles or more inferiorly on the anterior aspect of the public
bodies. Vertical and rotational displacement can be addressed by placing the tines in the
appropriate vector on either side of the pubic symphysis (Figure 15). Alternatively, a
Jungbluth clamp using two 3.5-mm screws as attachment pivot points may facilitate and
maintain reduction until definitive fixation is applied. This is especially helpful if anterior
or posterior translation of one hemipelvis relative to the other is required (Figure 16).
Four- or six-hole curved pelvic reconstruction plates can be used to stabilize the
reduction in many patients; however, thicker and more robust pre-contoured
symphyseal plates should be used in large patients and patients with obesity.

Posterior Pelvic Ring Reduction and Fixation Techniques

Posterior Pelvic Ring Reduction and Fixation Techniques
Depending on the individual characteristics of the injury pattern and soft-tissue
considerations, the posterior pelvic ring can be approached percutaneously or via an
open approach from anterior or posterior (Video 2).
Video 2 Rout ML Jr: Posterior pelvic solutions, from Kleweno CP, mod: Management of
pelvic fractures. Presented at the Annual Meeting of the American Academy of
Orthopaedic Surgeons, New Orleans, LA, March 6-10, 2018.
Type B injuries with sacroiliac joint disruption frequently can be reduced indirectly via
open reduction of the anterior pelvic ring, which may rotate the unstable hemipelvis into
more appropriate alignment. For example, if radiographs demonstrate a reduced (or

sacroiliac joint in patients with a pure type B injury (APC type II) are not well delineated in
the literature and remain controversial. If indirect reduction via manipulation of the
anterior pelvic ring is unsuccessful in aligning the posterior pelvis, then the surgeon
should proceed with open reduction.
Complete sacroiliac joint disruptions (type C injuries as in APC type III) and iliac wing
fractures can be reduced from anterior with the patient in the supine position through
the lateral window (window No. 1) of the ilioinguinal or iliofemoral approach. These
approaches can be supplemented with an osteotomy of the anterior superior iliac spine
to improve surgical access for placement of reduction clamps and internal fixation.
Various clamps and techniques are available for open reduction of sacroiliac joint
dislocations and iliac fractures via the anterior approach. Large bone forceps, pointed
tenaculum Weber clamps, or angled-jaw clamps that are used for other extremity
fractures can be used in the pelvis; they rely on having the ability to grasp the fragments
in opposition and compress. For example, an angled-jaw clamp, such as the gooseneck
clamp, requires one tine to be placed lateral to the iliac crest and the other tine to be
placed on the sacrum (Figure 17). In many pelvic fractures, this is not possible, and the
surgeon may elect to use Farabeuf (Figure 18) or Jungbluth (Figure 19) clamps that
involve the use of two 3.5-mm screws placed on either side of the dislocation or fracture
to directly manipulate each side of the injury in multiple planes.

For sacroiliac joint dislocations, percutaneous fixation with the use of iliosacral lag
screws can be performed in isolation or as a supplement to anterior sacroiliac plate
fixation. For iliac wing fractures, fixation often depends on the configuration of the
fracture and involvement of the sacroiliac joint. Pure iliac wing fractures that exit into the
greater sciatic notch anterior to the sacroiliac joint can be fixed with the use of a
combination of plates and screws at the level of the crest and the pelvic brim. With
increasing levels of sacroiliac joint involvement, supplemental iliosacral lag screws also
may be used.
Open reduction, clamp placement, and application of plate/screw fixation via an anterior
approach to the posterior pelvis require a keen understanding of the regional
neurovascular anatomy, particularly the L5 nerve root. The L5 nerve root is located a
mean of 2.3 cm medial to the sacroiliac joint more proximally on the ala but as little as
1.3 cm more distally.7 Therefore, plates should be placed posterior and superior to the
ala to prevent injury to the L5 nerve root. In most patients, only one screw can be placed
medial to the sacroiliac joint (Figure 20). In situations in which iliosacral screws are not
an option, at least two anterior sacroiliac plates should be used.

Displaced sacral fractures not amenable to closed reduction and percutaneous fixation
require open reduction via a posterior approach with the patient in the prone position.
Iliac wing fractures and sacroiliac joint dislocations also can be reduced via posterior
approaches to the pelvis; however, because of the higher wound complication rate and
inability to simultaneously manipulate the anterior pelvic ring, anterior approaches
generally are preferred by most surgeons for the iliac wing and the sacroiliac joint.
Sacral fractures are exposed via a midline or paramedian incision that elevates the
transverse fibers of the gluteus maximus and the paraspinal muscles from medial to
lateral. Various reduction techniques often are used to reduce a sacral fracture. The
patient should be positioned with the pelvis hanging freely and gentle longitudinal
traction applied through a distal femoral traction pin if the knee is flexed and hip
extended to relax the sciatic nerve. A 5-mm Schanz pin can be inserted in the posterior
superior iliac spine, directed toward the anterior inferior iliac spine, and used as a
joystick to aid in gross reduction. Large Weber clamps are then used to fine tune and
compress the fracture, with one tine on the spinous process of the sacrum and another
tine variably positioned on the lateral cortex of the ilium, depending on the vector
required (Figure 21). Alternatively, a large Jungbluth clamp with one 4.5-mm screw in
each posterior superior iliac spine is a powerful method for correcting rotation and

After satisfactory reduction of the sacrum is attained, percutaneous iliosacral or
transsacral screws can be placed across the fracture to stabilize the reduction. If vertical
or cranial instability is present, multiple points of fixation across the first and second
sacral segments are recommended. Based on individual anatomic considerations, this
may be a combination of iliosacral and transsacral screws. In situations in which multiple
screws cannot be safely placed across the fracture, sacral fixation should be augmented
with the use of a lumbopelvic construct or via transiliac plating. If spinopelvic
dissociation is present (bilateral alar fractures with a transverse component—type U or
type H sacral fracture), lumbopelvic fixation also may be necessary to prevent loss of
reduction, anterior translation, and a progressive kyphotic deformity during the course
of healing (Figure 22; Resource 4).

Technical Considerations for Placement of Posteriorly Based Screws
Numerous screw trajectories can be used to place percutaneous screws across the posterior
aspect of the pelvis and sacrum.
In general, transsacral screws are used to stabilize sacral fractures, and iliosacral screws are
used to stabilize sacroiliac joint dislocations (Resource 5).

Technical Considerations for Placement of Posteriorly Based Screws
Fixation is placed perpendicular to the fracture or joint surface as observed on inlet and
outlet views (Figure 23). Ultimately, patient anatomy, the injury pattern, and the
direction of displacement dictate the trajectory of the screws. Partially threaded or fully
threaded large-caliber (6.5 mm or greater) cannulated screws are most commonly used.

An understanding of normal variations in sacral anatomy is critical to the safe placement
of posterior fixation in the pelvic ring. Two types of sacral anatomy are commonly
encountered—normal and dysmorphic—depending on the position of the first sacral
segment relative to the sacral ala (Table 2). In a normal sacrum (Figure 24), the first
sacral segment is centered between the alae such that a straight bony corridor exists
across the entire S1 segment. In a dysmorphic sacrum (Figure 25), the first sacral
segment is positioned anterior and cephalad to the alae, such that a transsacral corridor
does not exist. In dysmorphic sacra, only iliosacral style screws are possible in the first
sacral segment. The two variations of sacral anatomy are best observed on outlet
radiographs.8

A concise understanding of pelvic landmarks on fluoroscopic images is critical during
percutaneous placement of screws across the posterior aspect of the pelvis. The two
main fluoroscopic views used intraoperatively are inlet and outlet views. A midsagittal CT
scan can be used to estimate the angles of inlet and outlet intraoperative fluoroscopic
images (Figure 26). The outlet view typically is obtained to visualize the foramena en face
and the superior end plate of S1. The inlet view typically is obtained to visualize the
anterior cortex of the first and second sacral segments. These views should be
confirmed by over- and under-adjusting the tilt to verify that an optimal inlet view has
been obtained to visualize the anterior cortex of the S1 or S2 segment (Figure 27). A
lateral sacral fluoroscopic image is the only view that affords visualization of all the
boundaries of the safe corridor; therefore, if any doubt exists with regard to safe

Outcomes

Outcomes
Current best evidence on pelvic fracture outcomes remains of low quality. A recent
meta-analysis reported no randomized controlled trials, four case-control studies, and
24 case series, concluding that the “existing literature in this area is inadequate to inform
surgeons or patients in a meaningful way about the functional outcomes of these
fractures.”9 Despite these limitations, a great deal remains to learn and build on from
within the previously published outcomes of pelvic injuries.
Nonsurgical Management Outcomes

Nonsurgical Management Outcomes
Literature on the nonsurgical management of pelvic ring injuries is sparse and
heterogenous. A meta-analysis spanning the literature from 1975 to 2007 identified only
four historical reports, with a mean year of publication of 1986.10 In this combined
series, most injuries were vertical shear injuries, a pattern that, currently, rarely is
considered for nonsurgical management. The results of this historic cohort can be
summarized as follows:
Quality of reduction reported as excellent (<5-mm displacement): 46%
Union rate: 83%
Malunion rate: 30.3%
Infection rate: 6.7% (all open injuries)
Severe pain: 27%
Normal gait: 68%
Return to work: 75.5%

A more recent study focused on 50 patients with a complete sacral fracture secondary to
a lateral compression injury and less than 1 cm of displacement.11 Mean physical and
mental component scores of the Medical Outcomes Study 12-Item Short were 48.8 and
48.9, respectively, which are very close to those of the population norm (50). The mean
Majeed Pelvic Outcome score was 85.5 (excellent). Additional clinical outcomes and
findings from this series included the following:
Union rate: 100%
Lower extremity numbness/paresthesias: 10%
Urinary incontinence: 6%.
Erectile dysfunction: 6%
These results led to the conclusion that acceptable results can be achieved via
nonsurgical management of this isolated injury pattern.
Surgical Management Outcomes

Surgical Management Outcomes
The quality and volume of literature on the surgical management of pelvic ring injuries
surpasses that of nonsurgical management, but with its own limitations. A recent meta-
analysis identified a total of 24 cohorts (1,488 patients) of surgically managed pelvic ring
injuries previously reported in the literature.10 Eight of these cohorts were managed
exclusively via anterior fixation (internal or external) and 16 of these cohorts were
managed via posterior fixation (open or percutaneous) with or without anterior fixation.

Complications

Complications
Traumatic pelvic ring injuries may lead to numerous complications resulting from the
injury itself and surgical management. Therefore, a thorough preoperative assessment
of potential urologic, vascular, and neurologic injuries should be performed to identify
any related injuries and deficits that were a direct result of the injury.
Postoperative wound infection and dehiscence are most notable after open posterior
approaches, particularly because internal degloving and soft-tissue injuries usually are
located posteriorly. Infection develops in very few patients who undergo percutaneous
fixation. Wound erythema without drainage within the first 2 weeks postoperatively can,
in most patients, be managed via a 2-week course of antibiotic agents; however, the
treating surgeon should have a low threshold for returning to the operating room for
irrigation and débridement of the wound, particularly if wound drainage or
hematoma/seroma formation is noted in combination with erythema or cellulitis. A CT
scan with contrast can be obtained to assess for deep fluid collections; however,
postoperative hematoma may be difficult to differentiate from an infected seroma.
Surgeon should err on the side of caution. If infection is suspected after the 3-month
mark and the fracture has healed, the surgeon should consider removal of implants.
Inflammatory markers, such as erythrocyte sedimentation rate and C-reactive protein
level, are useful to trend the status of the infection.
In patients with an external fixator pin-site infection, the patient should undergo a 2-
week course of oral antibiotic agents that cover gram-positive organisms; however, if the
pins are loose, lucency is present around the pins within the bony pelvis, or the infection
is not improving via oral antibiotic agents, then they should be removed, débrided, and
replaced to prevent osteomyelitis and a septic hip joint.

The most commonly noted failure of implants concerns plate breakage or screw
loosening across the pubic symphysis. Although reports of plate failure range from 12%
to 31%, plate failure does not appear to correlate with functional outcomes.15,25,26
However, surgeons must inform patients preoperatively that plate failure can occur
because of the natural motion that occurs at the symphysis. This will avoid unnecessary
anxiety if the finding is observed on postoperative radiographs. Retrograde ramus
screws are associated with a higher failure rate compared with antegrade ramus
screws.27 This is most notable for parasymphyseal fractures that have limited bone stock
for screw fixation on the near end of the fracture if fixed in retrograde fashion.
Newly diagnosed postoperative neurologic deficits may be a challenge to manage. In
many patients, a preoperative neurologic examination cannot be performed and the
surgeon is uncertain if the neurologic deficit is from the injury or the surgical procedure.
Patients with a new postoperative neurologic deficit should undergo CT of the pelvis to
verify safe placement of all implants and rule out impingement from fracture fragments.
Injury to the L5 and S1 nerve root may be related to implant positioning and reduction
techniques that may have placed the nerve on tension, especially in patients with a
nerve that was injured during the initial insult.
Conclusion

Conclusion
Pelvic ring disruptions may be some of the most challenging injuries orthopaedic
surgeons manage. This diverse group of injuries requires constant communication
between multiple subspecialties not only from a treatment standpoint but also from a
research standpoint.
